The lighting reptrictions naturally deprive us this year of that most enjoyable sensation—a stfoll through brilliantly illuminated streets— looking into gaily deeorated shop windows and being knocked about. by a wave of good- humoured, festive humanity. While there is no superabundant gaiety, let us hope' that there will be some modicum of happiness for each and every one. It is only right and proper that the gloomy veil should be raised ever so little, and that the season of goodwill Should not pass alto- gether unnoticed. This applies more particu- larly to the younger folk, on whom sorrow sits ligtitly. They should have a good chance in the afternoons of investigating the fascinating treasures of the toyshops while their tongues are busy with the sugary juices of the sweeties. One adage should be remembered by all—Shop early and often!

div.head: PRESENIS FOR ALL.
div.p: PRESENIS FOR ALL.
Afternoon Shop-Gazing For The Young Folk.

A little boy, young in years, but unlimited in imagination, was beard to ask if Santa Claus will be able to dodge the. Zepps this year. Of course, the answer was easy. Santa Claus is in- visible to wicked people, and only makes his calls on little folk who are good and well be- haved. Be his visits many or few, Christmas- tide is with us once again, and the hearts of most juveniles are trembling with anticipation as to what the great day may bring forth. Our soldier and sailor lads are, of course, our first thought, and one need only stand for a few minutes in front of one of our fine shops to see how varied are the useful articles and comforts which- we might send hini—if we only had the mopey. Much or little, however, there are goods and remembrances to suit all purses, and we hope that every " Tommy " and " Jack " will receive some useful article or kindly token to show that he is' ever present in the minds of those at home.

div.p: MODERN WITCHtS,
Making Fortunes Out of Telling
Fortunes.
ENORMOUS PRACTICE IN WARRINGTON.

One can hardly speak to a member of the fair sex in Warrington without her finally confessing that she has visited- one or other of the fortune tellers who are rampant in our midst Despite the recent declaration of the magistrates that it is nothing but folly and ignorance which lead people to wait upon fortune tellers, the majority of clients veritably believe that which• is uttered by these goddesses of wisdom these Solomons and Baron Munchansens of feminin- ity.

-Investigation by "The Examiner" man has disclosed the fact that there are about a dozen women in Warrington carrying on the trade of fortune telling. In order to record his im- pressions, he took steps with the object of going through the process, but has been unable to manage it. Fortune tellers 'know how to pre- serve their own fortunes. They absolutely de- cline to treat with people who are not intro- duced to them by others who have sat at their feet in credulous attitude. It would have been necessary for "The Examiner' man to have been formally introduced to a wizard by one previously associated with her. So much under the influefice of these women are their clients that they refuse to introduce one likely to ex- pose their methods. As showing the nervousness and yet persist- ency with which the business is carried on, one might say that as soon as the fortune tellers discover that their callers are genuine and friendly disposed, they are asked to bring along their friends—' But, mind you, don't bring any traitors!" is the injunction. It is this strategy which has surrounded them with almost im- pregnable fortifications, and the police are to be congratulated on having stormed two places a week or two ago, with the result that their cap- tives had to forfeit ..25 each.

div.head: RICH AND POOR EQUALLY DELUDED.
div.p: THE RICH AND POOR EQUALLY DELUDED.

As has been stated, as far as is ascertainable, there are about twelve of these wonien carrying on the trade in Warrington, either by means of palmistry, cards, or tea leaves in cups. Some haffe got an/ enormous clientile, not just from the artisan and alleged unthinking classes, but those of the upper classes also. At one place Quite a "classy" trade is done. Motor Mrs occa- sionally drive to the house—situated in Latch- ford—and fashionably dressed ladies descend to hear the story of their future. Other well=to-do ladies who wish to come into contact with the wizards, but have not the . boldness or con- descension to visit the headquarters, invite the " Futurists " into their great homes for tea, and extend the invitation to others in society to meet the women with the fatetpl cards. ' But it is amongst the workitit class girls that the practice is continued with such regularity as to have become a habit. It is not merely a matter of girls visiting these places occasionally, for many go week by. week, like youths going for a-shave. It is beyond dispute that'scores of the girls at Messrs. J. Crosfietd and Sons,' Ltd., march off, as soon as they have received their wages, to . notorious fortune teller in Bank Quay. By scores' of the pmployes' at Coekhedge Mills a similar routine ism's° gonethrough their establishment is not far' tiw,ay—they are not ex- hansted when they knock at the door and are ushered into "The Presence." A regrettable feature of these visits is that the patrons be- come models of credulity, having faith in every- thing heard, and unable to sort out the wheat— if there is any—from the chaff, of which there is a good deal. Possibly the most insidious feature is that vulgarity plays around delicate subjects. The incidents revealed in the Police Court proceedings are almost characteristic of every place.

The -war has brought fortunes,to many of the fortune tellers. It is upon the matrimonial stakes that they usually bat*, and now that sweethearts are at the Front girls go to these women with complete singleness of heart to find out their fate as revealed in a pack of cards.

"SOLDIERS FIGHTING FOR t s. d."

• Sir,—As the delegate of the British Workers' Nacional .League, i attended the kood Conter- ence held in the Co-operative nail on Thursday, December 7th. I wish to dissociate myself from the remarks made by one delegate, named Whitely, when tie said, "Al! the men that had gone to light had only gone for s. d." As one who has had two sons in. France, one of whom has given his life for his country, and the other being there still fighting, I feel it necessary to call Mr. Whitely to account, and ask him for an explanation of the statement. I was surprised the Chairman allowed Buell re- marks to be made, but what can you expect when he himself made insulting remarks about Unions having sold themselves politically.
So far as the Union of which I am the secre- tary in Warrington is concerned, we are not bound to any political organisation. As far as this conference was concerned we refused to
have any dealings with the local Ti4des Council because of their past conduct. It is time we
had real labour men on these bodies, not men of this stamp. When we tive, trade unions will unite, but there can be no real unity so long as Trades Councils act as this does. FREDERICK HODSON.

div.head: PACIFISM AND DRINKING.
div.p: PACIFISM AND DRINKING.

Sir,—ln hivermon on "Warrington and Free Speech," the Rev. H. Ogden declared that the "menace of the drink" was "one of the great- est enemies of this country at this time (beside which all peace proposals were insignificant)." Will you allow me to express my strong dis- agreement with these sentiments? Even exces- sive drinking—deplorable though it is—is de- cidedly less of a menace to the speedy prosecu- tion of the war to a full and final victory than the efforts of the pacifists to weaken the war- spirit of 'the people. But what about moderate drinking? High medical authorities—such as Sir James Crichton-Browne, &c.—tell us that the moderate use of alcohol is not only not injurious, but positively beneficial. Does the Rev. H. Ogden-contend that the man who drinks in moderation without harming, others and with benefit to himself is a greater danger to the nation than the pacifist who tries to bring about a premature peace, pleasing to the Germans and fatal to the aims of the Allies? I think Mr. Ogden would do Vetter to attack the menace of pacifism, instead of indulging in indiscriminat- ing denunciations of the use of alcoAol.
S. SIMPSON
December 12th, 1916.

div.head: LIBERAL SOCIAL.
div.p: LIBERAL SOCIAL.
Alderman Tinnion Praises Mr. Lloyd George.
The Warrington Women's Liberal Association

held another very successful ward social on Monday evening, when about one hundred and fifty people from the Whitecross and St. Aus- tin's Wards assembled in the John Crosfield Memorial Hall. The respective ward captains, Mrs. Israel and Mrs. •Balmford (for St. Aus- tin's) and Mrs. J. Percival (Whitecross), along with their energetic committee, had made suit- able arrangements which could not but command success. Whist, dominoes, and other 'games were played, a capable M.C. for the first- named being Mr. J. Percival. Refreshments were served during an interval, when. prizes to the successful whist and domino players were presented by Mrs. Locker. The winners were as follows :—Whist--Ladies: 1, Mrs. Clayton; 2, Mrs. Jones. Gents.: 1, Mr. Fleming; 2, Mrs. Johnson (playing as a gentle- man). Dominoes: 1, Mrs. J. Weston; 2, Mrs. Whittaker.
• Prizes had been kindly given by Alderman Tinnion, Councillors H. Roberts; G. Dale and J. T. Barton, and Messrs. T. Loeker, Bibby, White and P. Maginn.
• The pianist was Mr. G. S. Pendlebury. In the course of a short speech, Alderman Ennion referred to the unavoidable absence,

through illness, of Mrs. Osborne, their energetic secretary. He was sure he would be voicing the feelings of all present in wishing her a speedy recovery. He thanked Mrs: Locker for so kindly and charmingly presenting the prizes. There were several ladies present, he said, whom they could never ask too ften to do something for a good. cause. They were doing all they could to help the soldiers and sailors, and many others, in this terrible war.

Referring to the recent change of Govern- ment, Alderman Jinnion said that one of the head men in it was Mr. Lloyd George, a man of whom they were exceedingly proud. (Hear, hear.) He had, undoubtedly, on more than one occasion, by his driving power and clear, think- ing, done as much and probably more than any. 'other' Man. He' (the speaker) could only hope that, as a nation, the people-would do all they could to assist that Government in bringing the war to a. successful conclusion. "I think we all have relations," said the speaker, "who are prepared—some of them have already done so— to lay down their lives for this glorious Empire for which we are fighting. Knowing the true sentiments of the people of St. Austin's and Whitecross Wards, I know you will put the country's well-being before everything else When the war is over and the political feelings of the country come to be registered, I hope St. Austin's and Whitecross Wards will be found in the van and leading on to victory." (Ap- plause.)

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
Desecration.

Lest any should imagine that the robbery of graves commented upon in last week's " Gossip" is peculiar to these parts, let me hasten to state that the like disgraceful practices have been fairly common in other localities in which I have lived. The poets, Thomson .particularly, insist upon the sacredness of the human remains that lie within the .tomb; but .these most miser- able of thieves are incapable of being touched by any such appeals. One caught in the act— and one may well suggest that detection should not be difficult—ought to be severely punished as an example.

"The Queen of Night." Artemus Ward, the genial showman, had, or professed to have, his " moonist " for panoramic purposes. So, apparently (vide local intelli- gence) has the "Examiner." So much the better. Time was when comparatively few con- cerned themselves with such phenomena as the direction of the wind for the time being and the phases of the moon. But the lighting re: strictions have altered all that, and the Phcebe or Cynthia of the poets is once more hailed as,, "goddess, sov'reign of the night." I am re minded of a period when it fell to my lot to " do " the district for a Yorkshire paper, and the country folk regulated their meetings by, the almanaek. Some of the older Oddfellows' lodges in what have become Quite large towns meet "on the Monday nearest to full moon." Well, the old rule may serve its original purpose during wartime.

" Sci2nce and Industry." ,Dr. Hilditch's lecture under this title on Monday set me thinking of the extraordinary patience of the scientific man. How careful he is—how precise—how patiently he waits! That eminent authority on synthetic chemistry, the late Professor Berthelot, foretold the coming of a time when deserts would be the most desirable localities on the earth, "thanks to their salu- brity as compared with th9,4kestiferous alluvia and putrefying plain's that k-,/now the favoured seats of, our agriculture." According to this learned enthusiast, the chemist was to take the place of Nature, and make in his "lab." every- thing we require, food included. Had the lamented professor been granted a! longer lease of life, possibly ere this we might have had tabloid joints, steaks, and chops—which, as a temporary expedient at least, would have been convenient in these times of heavy freightage and army transport. It was another professor (Professor llerries) who promised us a perfect indiarubber ,substitute from certain hydro- carbon compounds. To be sure, there were some substitutes for, the precious rubbdr already on the market. In one district in which I lived several years ago, extensive premises were built for, the manufacture of go- me such article, though that particular firm cleared out two or three years afterwards. Since then another chemist has put forward the claim to have made silver, but nothing came of it. However, the science of organic chemistry is moving along, and is destined to perform many seeming miracles. The Weather.

I must not allow our friendly " Critic " to have the last word as to this; it is too good a topic to be lightly regarded. I think it was " S.L.FI." who wrote in his wonderful column —now as "emphatically' defunct" as Mark Twain's camel—that he suspected anyone who pretended to take no interest in the weather, even as Charles Lamb thought that no man who said " No " when offered apple-dumpling could be pure-minded. The first article of his that appeared in print was on this subject, and in it he pointed out that Shakespeare recognised that indifference to the weather characterised a' villain. When poor Banquo says, as any gentle- man at the dinner table might say when trying to start conversation, "It will be rain to-night," he receives the brutally callous answer, "Let it come down," an answer showing that the fellow who uttered it cared nothing about the weather. The history of the good fairy who is supposed to visit virtuous little boys and girls and to leave with them the con- tents (or part of them) of the local toy-shops, is another example of the borrowing' of custom from foreign lands. He is really a curious mixture of the legends of a medieval Saint Nicholas, a boy-bishop .irho was said to have gone round amongst children re- warding the good. div.head: CHARLIE CHAPLIN.
div.p: CHARLIE CHAPLIN.
Boyish Impersonations In The
Streets.

Affected to a degree of emulation by the cine- matographic antics of Charlie Chaplin, a couple of Warrington boys succeeded in. impersonating him the other evening. In their peregrinations round the town they were objects of curiosity, and, like a recruiting band during the Derby scheme, got a good following. ' I saw one of them giving a performance in Winwick-street (writes an " Examiner " observer). He was walking and tumbling about with wonderful facility. Several of his pals attended him as " supers " and enjoyed the way in which he ran up against them or struck them with his stick, and then apologised by snapping off his hat, simultaneously maintaining a solemn face and without uttering a word. He looked the exact replica of Charlie, having borrowed the necessary equipment—a bowler hat, resem- bling a bricklayer's by reason of its contorted shape and surface of dust; and his father's working trousers and boots. Not being able to borrow or grow a moustache, the stroking of a burnt cork across his upper lip had gained the effect desired. With a light cane in his hand and a simple, melancholy and mute expression on his face, you had Charlie right enough, walk- ing on those stiff legs of his—his feet at an angle of 120 degrees—and falling about in the ,requis- ite haphazard manner, caring not where or how

he- bumped. Passers-by looked at him and re- marked to each other, "There's Charlie Chap- lin! Hi! Hi! Hi!" The famous actor ap- proached in ;the famous actor's sstyle of peram- bulation, raised his hat and then lowered it to the third button of his waistcoat; where he rested it, and hoped that soon he would he able to rattle it with coins. But, generally, the passers-by passed on. stopped to pat a ques- tion to him.
"Would you like to be the real Charlie Chap- :n?" I asked.

To speak would be a violation of Charlie's character (with Charlie silence is golden—when before the film operator), and the boyish, im- personator hesitated to do that, but eventually he exclaimed, "Would I!" in quiet, envious tones.

"Would you like .1:500 a week?" "Would I!" His tone was Still envious.
"What would yo do with it?'

It was evident that he had not contemplated such a dazzling prospect, and it -was only after deep thought that he answered, "I'd buy a horse and cart and a motor car "—one happened to be passing at the time. Her disdained the Longford car. "Would you still live round here?"
"Would I! I'd go to London and make 'em build me a house—l mean a palace—like the King's." "What would you do with the rest of the money?" _ _
"I'd give a bit to the poor and the war."
"What else would'you-do?"
He was stuck for an idea, and by looking heavenwards (Or Zep-wards) eventually got one. "I'd give my mother the rest," he said sud- denly.
"'Very good, sonny," I remarked. "Here' sixpence. You can have that for yourself."

, What those in the Army think of Germany's offer of peepe. is vital, and, ;therefore, the fol- lowing contribution, specially written for "Tire Examiner," should be read with great interest. It is penned by Private Peter F. Somerville, of the Royal Fusiliers, who, before crossing to France in khaki, -.served there' as war correspondent to a Series of _important newspapers. At one, time he was a colleague of our Chief Reporter. He has been. wounded and lies in. 'hospital' with a paralysed arm-7- fortunately, his left. One is glad to notice that he 'still retains his freshness, of outlook and style. He writes There may be some people ,in 'this country who are satisfied that the British soldier is too much a soldier to be moved by talk of peace. • Should the belief lie anywhere held it need occasion, no surprise. Since August, 1914, we have been living in: a world Of make- believe'. Nothing is 'exactly what it seems. We are not permitted-to think 'calmly and justly , about the German, about; the Bul- garian, about ourselves.•, Not the least of the evils of the war is that it has for, the moment submerged truth. The Dream of Peace.

So far from the British. soldier feeling above all talk of peitce, it is the one thing he dreams about. If peace. should ,be declared with the British and German- armies still confronting one another, there ,would, I 'venture to think, he scenes of. Anglo-Gernian fraternity that would stagger .students of international rela- tionships and puzzle them to. the end of their days. This is because war means so much more to the man who is engaged in it. A "gallant British advance "-may mean for him going short of food or water, spending hours in mud to the knees, enduring the last tor- ments of fatigue; and facing continually— facing it once would,he easy, almost pleasant— the possibility of a violent death, or worse, in .an obscure corner of a desblate battlefield. One may say as much with Out any complaint against our organisation, which is good, Or without modifying one's belief in the splendid soldierly qualities of the typical Englishman, and his zeal for a fine cause. It is merely the admission that he is human, and not a machine. And. because he is human, what England at home ' may think or do touches him. -

div.head: Our Clcar Duty.
div.p: Our Clcar Duty.

It is essential that we should not conclude peace merely because we feel tired of the war. We are not children, and .the war is not a toy. Peace ought to come when we are satis- fied that we have done all we think we ought to have done. This means courage and dis- cipline everywhere. If there is war-weariness among those living in comfort at home, be assured it is not unknown at the Front. The clear duty of those living, in safety is to stimulate the courage and steel the determina- tion of those whose lot is the harder so that diplomatic offers of peace. by .Germany may he appreciated 'at their real worth. This offer of peace comes- from. the old German heart. It will be time to think .seriously. Of peace when we detect in the German tone 'a more honest ring. Meanwhile the cry of' the ,soldier from across the Channel might Well be: "Help tiS! Encourage us to look steadily ahead to the end of our task. It us feel that the cause is worth the effort, and that England is 'worth saving. Help us to feel that a life lost in the struggle will not be forgotten, so that when the unutterable longing for peace is realised and We •return again to the world of little children, of books, of •th 6 music of tea- cups, of peaceful family relationships, it will be with the consciousness of duty done; that we have not been unfaithful to • the trust bequeathed to us by Drake and Nelson.'

div.head: To the Editor of "The Examiner."
div.p: To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,.--While Germany's peace terms are defined neither in the Chancellor's speech in the Reich- stag, nor in the communication addressed to the Allies through the neutral States, the note struck throughout Herr von Bethmann-Htll- wegg's speech makes it abundantly and conclu- sively evident that the only peace terms Ger- many contemplates at this juncture are terms which the Allied nations will be utterly unable to accept. A patched-up peace on Germany's terms at the present time would leave the mili- tary caste of Prussia still in the saddle and able to dominate the whole of Central Europe.

Besides # population of more than 80,000,000 of Austro-Germans, it is the evident and .certain intention of the Prussian autocracy to estalilish absolute ascendancy for all military and diplo- matic purposes over something like 100,000,000 of people that dwell in that part of Europe which extends from the Poles at one end to the Roumanians, Bulgars and Greeks at the other end—an Empire which would control Constan- tinople and the Dardanelles, and carry its sway through Asia Minor into Mesopotamia. That once achieved, nothing would -stop them pursu- ing their plans for world, domination, and we know already from experience just how much reliance could be placed upon any treaties entered into by Germany which were calculated to interfere with pan-German schemes of ag- gression whenever the rulers of Germany saw, or thought therlsaw, their opportunity to strike again.

div.head: OUR ONLY TERMS.
div.p: OUR ONLY TERMS.

As to the Allies' terms in their general outline, Germany knows them well enough, but in all probability this demarcbe made by the Imperial Chancellor will lead to a statement by the Allied Powers which will make it clear to the people of those nations, to the neutral States, and last but not least, to the people of the Central Empires, that the door is open for negotiations for peace the moment the Prussian authorities are ready to recognise that no terms can be entertainEd by the Allies which do not include recognition of the rights of nationalities, great and small, adequate reparation for what has happened, and -absolute security with regard to the future. Complete reparation? No; we shall not stipulate for that, for two reasons: first, because. it is utterly beyond the power of Germany and Austria to make complete repara- tion for ~tho frightful crime they have com- mitted; and secondly, beeauseit has been made clear that; so far as Britain at any rate is. con- cerned, it is no purpose of ours to prolong the horrors of war by a single day - in. order to pursue a vindictive policy to the bitter. end. There is unhappily no prospect whatever of peace on such terms at the present time. , The pride of the Prussian autocracy has still to be broken, and can only be broken by the continued pressure of the Allied Fleets•and Armies. That is a terrible fact, but it is a fact to be faced with iron resolution hr the whole of our people; and at such a time meetings held .to advocate the ratification of a premature peace on terms which would be but a hollow, worthless piece of make- believe, and which would give •us no permanent security whatever—such meetings are to be most strongly deprecated. '

div.head: PEACE MEETINGS TO BE DEPRECATED
div.p: PEACE MEETINGS TO BE DEPRECATED

I do not know what Mr. Trevelyan proposed to say at the. small gatherink he was invited to address last Friday week, but fearing that the tenor of. his remarks,:sw,en,l4. he in the direction I have just- hid/tilted, I for . one strongly dissented from the , policy ,of those who had arranged ..the . meeting., , Since, how- ever, it was decided, to hold the meeting with the permission of the authorities, I entirely concur in the view expressed in Mr. Charles Parker's letter in. last Saturday's Exam- iner," that it was impolitic to give an intended meeting of that character such an -advertise- ment as it received on Friday week. Had the meeting. been held, and, had Mr. ,Trevelyan spoken at it as the advocate of weak and futile and therefore dangerous Peace terms,then, provided our local newepapers had 'de- clined to publish a syllable of what was said at it, no harm would -have been .done. But I should like to take this opportunity to regis- ter my, protest against holding, or attempting to hold, any public meetings of such a char- acter as I have indicated at the present time. for the simple reason that, they may acquire either publicity in the Press, or notoriety in other ways that is calculated to disgust those who are bearing the burden and heat of the day,,,j,be it on the-high seas. or at the Front, and to create some apprehension in their minds lest war weariness should begin to inspire nerveless counsels of weakness at home. We owe it to the .heroes• who are fight- ing, and to those who have ,fallen, and we owe it to their posterity and ours; and we owe it to our Allies to. make sure that there shall be no weakening -of our purpose, and that Peace. .when it comes, shall be such a Peace as will put it beyond the power of '.any man, or group of men, or nation, to inflict upon generations in the future a :repetition of the cataclysm of infamy and suffering which has overtaken the unhappy nations of Europe in our days.
WHAT MINORITIES MUST SACRIFICE.

• My old friend, Mr. 3laginn, puts in a timely plea for complete unity of action and purpose during this crisis. It is. happily, superfluous to add that such unity is unthinkable except on the common ground of whole-hearted support for ttiose who are fighting our battles in the field, watching with ceaseless vigilance

and toil over Britain's interests on the high seas—grappling, with dauntless courage and resolution, the formidable dangers to be faced there; and, finally, for those who are charged with the overwhelming responsibility of guiding the nation's destinies. The prin- ciples and policies that direct our actions in time of peace a-nd in a war like this cannot be identical. We are entitled to urge minor- ities to sacrifice for the moment, and for the moment only, something of that cherished British right of free speech which, in its entirety, with every othei form• of British liberty we are in the last resort and in ,the long run fighting in this war tO defend.— Yours, &c.,
A. H. CROSFIELD. 41. West Hill, Highgate, N. December 13th, 1916.

An American doctor holding an important offi- cial position in his own country, after spending some months in Belgium during the late sum- mer, reports very seriously on the condition of the young life of that afflicted conntry. • The chief points of his report may be summarised as follows :

To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,---To my mind it is lamentable to witness the. misplaced energy and special pleading which .n 4 critics have displayed in their efforts to 'Trove, that the " licence ". claimed by Mr. Trevelyan (to. give public utterance to'.senti- ments and idea's which are abhorrent to the vast majoritj, of our people, calculated to provoke serious disorder,. embarrassing ;to the Government and a menace to our n4tional well-being), is consistent with the "sanctity of free speech?' Mr. Trevelyan's 'offensive attitude is further grossly ',aggravated by the -fact-, that. he con- tinues to .; draw .2400 per annum from the , National Exchequer, after having betrayed ' his constituency, forfeited its confidence 'and refused to resign a position to 'which he has, no longer the slightest right. - I am indeed grieved to sO3 two. ,uch good friends of mine, as are Mr.. Ogden and Mr. Parker, . allowing their zeal to outrun, their, discretion in their championship of. so un-; 'worthy an individual .at a time "when: OS Mr. Parker says). we have all something , better to do." As. a ~-et-off against the illogical- and not .over-kind criticism of_ my two friends, whose attitude smacks just a " too- much .of the, style of the "superior -person," I have received :-expressions of approval of the aetion of, lnY friends and -myself from large 'anthers of our townsfolk, and last.- but not least; the cordial .appreciation of one whose friendship I .Value dearly and.-- whoee bravery and 'self- sacrifice have won for him the lasting grati- tude. :of .his King.' and country.. div.head: SUPPRESSED MEETING. To the Editor of "The Examiner."
div.p: THE SUPPRESSED MEETING. To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—The steps. taken to suppress the' meet- ing at which Mr. Trevelyan wars to have spoken were most, regrettable. .We know perfectly well the law-abiding. character: of the people to whom he' came to speak; it was not an isolated meeting, but one of a series, .which had been going on for .several monthe, and the interference came too late to be of any value. Meetings on, peace and non-combatant 'lines have been- held by the !' Friends" in their Meeting • Hotise, for many months past, and, however we may differ from them in our opinions, 'we.: may surely give them, credit for honesty of ...purpose. It. was at • least unnee- ftsary to. suppress 'them by. • mob law, Or an appeal to ,7 the Mayor. . The better course would have .been to allow the. meeting to •be held, .and if, anything was said worth 'answer- ing to .haveijaeld a reply meeting on a. sub- sequent .date.. Surely. we are not fighting for freedom: on ,the plains •of Europe, and at home suppressing the most law-abiding class of Our fellow-townsmen? The question needs no fur- ther argument: it is most .silly and imprudent in the extreme.—Yours, &e., 3 f.,; PHIL SQUOD.

div.head: COUNCILLOR DALE AND MR. OGDEN'S IDEALS. To 'the-Editor of "The Examinee."
div.p: COUNCILLOR DALE AND MR. OGDEN'S IDEALS. To 'the-Editor of "The Examinee."

Sir,.,--ttather from your' report .in reference to a recent fitilress 1 v the Rev: IL 'Ogden that the reverend gentleman wishes 'it' to be under- stood that h is a believer in free speed). What be means* by free speech is not clear, and there is a certain amount of •.emplia- -siSed'• ambiguity abOut hi S address • which creates ; a suSpicion that it was inspired by that Spirit .6f strong enthusiasm which is sometimes :isSeciated with -uncertainty. •. •

Mr. 0gd?..114a7Y.s :---"•The Rl:ere& right of free speech is IiSH vital ag ' truth; and truth "is as old as God," " and "there is no time when a ivan 'should .fkil to express all the truth that is in him." - , Yes; that sounds 'very • nice; but surely free 'Speech, -in - the .absolute sense; allows a man' to express things that, aceording. to our • recognised -standards; are downright bad, and that .are the very antithesis •of truth. Is free speech, in this enSe, it sacred right? As a matter of fact, Mr. Ogden does • not be- lieve in free -Speech. ,He seems • to 'stand forth as its ctampien, but, instead of fighting for it, he immediately gives if away, for he allows certain limitations and restrictions which Completely destroy his main argument!: If he sets biniself up as an expert and a. -judge in respect of • 'Ow -choice of these limitations, why should he deny the right to others; - who, in special circumstances, choose to • add eer- tain restriction's to those. that he himself has already 'recognised? Mr. Ogden ••must admit that in exceptional crises we may be juStified in proceeding- on exceptional line with regard to questions which in •• normal tithes/ we could' afford to ignore. '!--

-Those of us: Who organised the protest meet- ing are citizens of ' Warrington, who, while remaining in comparative comfort at honie, are greatly cOricerned that everything possible should be done to help those who are fighting our battles; also that everything possible should be done, to upset the . calculations. of those who have never lifted a finger to help England in this crisis, but have rather- taken advantage of 'every opportunity for creating embarrassment 4

Tell us We are out of order if you like! We cannot be ov.erlfastidions in these days. While our lads are suffering, fighting and dying' in tha trenches, and while from the battlefields of Eastern and Western Europe a great cry goes up ,to Heaven for vengeance, we cannot stand on ceremony, nor :can we :stay to, be over particular about conventionalism. Yes, but says Mr. Ogden,-!` this war will be a mere incident 100 years hence." Whatever it .may be 100 years hence, it is a mighty big incident to us who are -living, to-day, and we are not so certain, as Mr. Ogden appears to be, as to how people will regard it in a hundred years from now., . . . ,
Indeed, is it probable that this mighty up- heaval of civilisation, the like of which the world has never known, will, when .a century has passed, be looked upon as .a mere inci- dent? We think not!

The neurasthenic heritage alone which this terrible war wail bequeath will make itself painfully • felt through many generations. A repetition of anything like the present tragedy means handing on additional burdens to gener- ations tlt will be sufficiently handicapped without them. ; • , ' . ,

Mr. Henderson, who is a 'well-known Non- conformist 'and a member ,of the new Cabinet. said, in his _ speech last Monday night: I want to warn , everyone of the danger of a premature pea Ce. I am as strong for peat* as any man ' Or woman can be, but, I must be satisfied that the . peace we. expect Places us, Without any' doubt, beyond the recurrence of such a catastrophe:"—Yours, •
- G. DALE. 23, Lovely-lane, Deeetnber 13th, 1916.

Private James Jennings, Manchester Regi- ment, who .is at present "somewhere in Egypt," writing to his mother at Moston- street, says:— _

_ I received your most welcome letters on returning to camp from Cairo, where I have beep for the last month, undergoing- a course of instruction on • machine gunnery. The course lasted altogether about three weeks, and I. am very sorry it has finished. It was hard work, but it was far nicer than being in camp. I think anywhere is better than being here. for it is so dreary, and I don't think that there is a man among us but what wishes that they would send us to France, or, in fact, anywhere out of this. We have hardly a minute to ourselves, for we are at it from 'Reveille' to 'Lights out.' I passed out of the ,school as a first-class gunner, so my labours have/not been in vain, and it is all for a good cause. I found Cairo a very nice place, and it was quite a treat to get on a hard road again; but kt didn't half make my feet sore for a time. On arriving back to camp I found that my company had moved a few miles further out, so I had to follow on, and when I caught them, up I was just in time for another long march. Perhaps by the time you receive This letter we shall be hav- ing another do with "Johnny.' I cannot tell you any details, but I only hope and trust that we will come through all right.
First Rain For Ten Months.

"The, weather is still rather hot in the day, but it is not so hot as it used to be. It broke its 'duck' last week by raining. The first drop of rain for ten months. Phew! What a relief! "I wrote to William Taylor, in Egypt, and Jack Leigh, in Mesopotamia, but it appears they have both crossed over and exchanged places. By CRITIC.
Christmas now draws very near and It sup- pose you will all be very busy making the necessary preparations.

Having all dispatched your parcels of good cheer to "Jack" and "Tommy," you will naturally be thinking about home comforts. One can hardly imagine that this is the third Christmas of the war. How many more there will be one hardly dares to think.
How well I remember the first! Shall ever forget it?

As I lay in hosPital (a member of His Majesty's Forces) I heard the boys carolling outside; and as I write I wonder how many of those boys will carol this season. Christmas may be a time of cheer, but at the present it brings many sad recollections.
I heard my first lot of carollers the other evening. Several small boys were giving vent to "As I stood by my father's door." And all the time they stood at someone else's door!
Until the patience of the owner was ex- hausted; then, on spotting a dog approaching, they did the disappearing act.
I hear that a party of munitioneers from the Lancashire Tool ,Company intend to go out carolling this season. •
And what they "earn" is to be given to the local Red Cross Funds. I wish them the best of luck. for their cause is great.
"Christmas leave from Salonical." Such is the latest experience a one of our local soldiers.
Cyclists and motorists would be greatly obliged if the walking public would kindly keep to the footpaths .these dark nights.
And to avoid collisions I should advise them to keep to the left.
I hear a movement is on foot to try and get the railway company to issue workmen's tickets from Lymm to Warrington.
They already issue them from Warrington to Lymm. Why, I cannot tell! If this arrangement was reversed I am sure it would be a public convenience.
A local soldier writing from Egypt. says that there is still a chance of having a little Turk(ey) for dinnen at Christmas. Mind the dripping!

div.p: "A VOICE FROM GERMANY."
Local Soldier Who Will Welcome Prisoners' Parcels.

In view of the special appeals made for parcels for prisoners of war, one of which appeared in our last week's issue, we publish a letter re- ceived this week from Privitte Walter Massey, of the Gheohireitegixaent, who-was captured by the Huns during the memorable retreat from Mons. Writing to his parents at Rush Green he says: "Just a few lines to let you know that I am all right and in the pink, hoping everyone is keeping well at home. I am now back again from off the farm, and if you can send me a parcel or two I shall be very grateful, for I shall need them here I can assure you. I sup- pose you have not heard from Walter (a sol- dier pal) yet about that suit?- It's about time I got a pail, of pants anyhow. I expect that it will be :Mut Christmas when you get this letter, so here's wishing you a merry Christmas and a happy New Tear. I. do hope you will., have a good time. I shall have to be content at having mine when I get out of here, and I don't know when that will be; but roll on time, it will come some day." This letter just gives us an idea of how our 11 gallant lads are taking their misfortune, and it also gives-us an idea as to how acceptable parcels from home really are. We at home will sit down to a well-spread table this Christmas, but what sort of Christmas didner will our gallant lads out there get who are at the mercy of a treacherous enemy? It gives us • pain to I think, and we only hope that they have not been forgotten.

THE EXAMINER. SATURDA 1 , DECEMBER 16, 1916.
CHRISTMAS LEAVE FROM SALONICA:
Corporal George Stant Amongst The
First Arrivals.

Corporal George Stant, a popular member of the motor transport, has arrived home at Branch Cottages, Cherry-lane, on 14 days' Christmas leave from Salonica. Clad in full marching order, and laden with all his treasured posses- sions, he arrived at Lymm Station on the 10.5 train last Tuesday night: Talking to our repre- sentative on his way from the station,. he in- formed him that this is the first leave he has aad since he enlisted early in January, 1915. "We have," he said, "been on the road since the latter end of November. We came via France, and I can' assure you it was a terrible journey. We practically lived-on bully beef and biscuits all the time, and sometimes very little of that. During the last three days until I ar- rived at Warrington I have only had one pint of tea. Hello! Have you been having snow?" our representative replied, "just a little. Have you had any out Oerei" "No," he said, "only on the hills, butrl noticed they have had a little in France."

Taking stock of his great amount of luggage, he remarked that they were -forced to bring it. "It's, not because you want it," he remarked, "but if you left it behind it would (Yet lost, and that would mean paying for it, which would never do."

"Well, here we are," our representative re- matked, as Cherry-lane corner was turned. "Home once again." " Yes," •he replied; "thank God. Good- night, and thanks for your company." 'Corporal Stant was well known in Lymm before the war, and was a motor mechanic and driver for Mr. E. S. Straker, of the Cherry-lane Garage. It is interesting to note that Mr. Straker is at present on active service some- where in Egypt, and has been now for some considerable time. We have reason to believe that he is going on well and keeps in good health.

, Thursday was SpLec.i Day at zim Grammai School, and a large company assemuled on tilt invitation of the Governors and riead Mastei (t,aptain W. S. The big attraction provided for the visitors entertainment was a capital performance by the pupils ,of "A Midsummer igat's Dream." It was a really fine effort of memorising, whiles.th€ elocutionary powers of the young kerformers and their clearness of enunciation, show that the study of our native language has been given the foremost place it should occupy in an Eng- lish Grammar School. The production lasted over two hours, and reflected the highest credit on the Head Master's coaching. Mrs. Ridgway, Mrs. Kirk, Mr. George Williamson, and Mr. Oddie gave •valuable assistance in various matters of detail.

The Rev. G. B. Thurston, vicar of Lymm. chairman of the Board of Governors, presided, and with him on the platform were Mrs. Ridg- a*, Mr. Maxwell Garnett, the Rev. G. S. Tudor Evans (Oughtrington), and Mr. Alfred Watkin. Importance of Home Work.

Captain Hawkins, in his annual report, urged the necessity of studious home work and the cultivation of reading English aloud. The num- ber of pupils had been well maintained. ; For the three terms respectively there had beep 139 (74 boys and 65 girls), 147 (79 and 68), and 152 (79. and 72). There had been 42 new entries this term. The attendance had been much ineire satisfactory, and the school had fortunately been free from infection, in spite of prevailing epi- demics. The work of the Upper Forms was tested in July by the Northern Universities Joint Board. The examinations of that body were not yet as well known as the Oxford and Cambridge locals, but they were more widely adopted in the North of England. They brought schools into closer touch with those who con- trolled the courses at the Universities of Mita- chester, Liverpool, Sheffield and Leeds. Two pupils took the Matric. Examination; one, Ruth Willan, passed, and in higher papers in English language, French and history, the whole of Form A, average age 14.4 i, entered for the School Cefitificate Examination, and all were awarded certificates. The next Form, average 13.4, also took the examination. Two were ambi- tious enough to enter for the certificate, and one, Hallows, got it. Forms were entered as a whole, and were examined on the strength of the ordin- ary Form work. The examiners recognised good progress and fair attainment. The record in drawing was very satisfactory. The other Forms had been examined by the staff. Steady im- provement in French was reported, as well as in mathematics, science and English. Mr. Hawkins was glad that they were getting a better stan- dard in home work, and he was obliged to the parents for giving him notice when the amount appeared to be excessive--he said " appeared " because in some cases excessive zeal was sho*n one night to make up for the deficiencies of the night before. On the whole there was a keen spirit of work in the school; the tone- was healthy and happy, and their games were show- ing improvement in technique. They could play hard in a losing match to the end. The boys and girls had found time to do a little war work. Their roll of honour was' growing. Through his absence during the-year 1914, and comparatively recent arrival he was unfortunately not ac- quainted with many "old boys" serving, and he should be- grateful for any 'names that did not appear on. the list, and for particulars of their welfare. They were proud to record that W. Russell Jones, R.G.A., had been granted the Medaille d' Homieur, and that Mr. Redhead, after working his way up from private to ser- geant in the Manchesters, had been granted a commission. (Applause.) He was glad to say that although boys were leaving school at rather :an-early age,* they were not entering blind alley' employments, but were showing preference .for such as demanded further education. ," May I; in conclusion," said Mr. Hawkins, "offer the thanks of the school to donors-of valuable gifts —to the Chairman for 20 books; to Miss Ridgway for 50 books from -the library of the late Lieut. Althorpe Ridgway, who died of mounds received in Gallipoli; to Mr. Sidney Davies for a fur- ther present of hangings for the stage; and to Mr. Pearson for seeds for the girls' hockey field. Varied, most valuable, and welcome gifts." (Applause.)

div.head: MILK AND ITS PRICE.
div.p: MILK AND ITS PRICE.
Suggestions For Regulating Supply And Cost.
DAIRY FARMERS' PROFITS
To the Editor of " The Examiner."

Sir,—l note with, pleasure the suggestion in Mr. Maginn's letter in your issue of December 9th—and I. wish to support and supplement it —" that his Worship the Mayor should call a meeting of re.sponsible citizens of every class to further unity of action." I expect he, and others interested in such a meeting, will have some definite subjects to propose calling for united action. If not, I fear the meeting will be like an eloquent sermon I once heard on Heaven: it told of its joy, its peace, its lrappiness. its beauties; but quite forgot to tell us how to get there. I would respectfully suggest that our milk supply and the present prices charges would be a subject worthy of the consideration of such a meeting. I think all *will admit that to place a full supply of new milk at a reasonable price within the 'reach of our workers with families of children would be one of the greatest bene- fits that could be conferred on our city; and I see no reason why this could not be done if a small Business Committee was appointed to take the matter in hand.

I suggest that a reasonable price Would be Id. per quart, and that a full supply could be brought from districts where milk is made into butter, or from Ireland, to supplement locai supplies. The present price charged is WI. or 6d. per quart. So that any family buying less than a quart pays at the rate of 6d. High Price Not Warranted.

I submit, and hope to prove, that 6d. per quart is not warranted by the present condi- tions or prices of feeding stuffs. This price is due more to the faulty and expensive methods of distribution from house to house than to the high prices paid to the producers. They do not get 6d. per quart, unless they also distribute the milk from house to house. But if the retail price of 6d. per quart is justifiable the producer should get at least qd. per quart, is. 6d. per gallon wholesale (this allows (Id. per gallon for carriage, distribution and profit to dealer), but the majority of farmers do not get anything like this price: is. 2d. to Is. 3d. per gallon would be nearer the average price; and where milk is turned into butter is. nor gallon would be the most it &raid yield, even _with butter 2s. per lb. or over. _ _ _
_ The question will be asked: "Does is. 2d. per gallon pay the producer, considering the high prices he has to pay for cake, grains and other feeding stuffs?" My answer is "Yes."

No up-to-date farmer will keep a dairy of Cows that will give him less, on the average, than 600 gallons of milk per cow per year, at is. 2d. per ga110n=.235. The cost for feeding, milking and tending a cow for a year would not be more than £2O, which leaves a net profit of ,21.5 per cow. So that a dairy of 40 cows would bring in a net income of .2600 per year to its owner.

I suggest that if local producers are paid is. 2d. per gallon•for.railk delivered at a depot in Warrington it would pay them well, and that this milk could be scld from depots (not house to house) at 4d. per quart, and if enough local producers could not be found to give a full supply, milk could be brought from other districts, or Ireland, at or near this price. I was told on good authority that the price paid' in Wiltshire for--milk delivered at many large dairies is Is. Id. per gallon, and in the South of Ireland thousands of gallons of milk are delivered to the creameries at Bd. and 9d. per gallon. This milk could be brought into Warrington within twelve hours, or less, and would Arrive about 6 o'clock each morning, and could be sold retail from depots; after paying carriage and expenses. at 4d per quart, and that it would be as good and sweet as any produced locally. In fact, thousands of gallon A are sent each week to London, and it arrives in splendid condition. I am prepared to give any committee inter- ested much fuller particulars that cannot be included in a letter, and do anything in my power to brill,'b such a scheme into existence, as I believe it would confer untold benefits on the workers of our city and neighbourhood.— Yours, Zio.,
A. COLE.

div.head: WAR BREAD.

In lad week's "-Facts and Fancies" "Critic" referred to the sale of war flour, but we an now state that the actual !war bread is being used throtighout the village. .A. prominent local baker tells our representative that his firm com- menced using- the national flour last Saturday with little or no effect on the public. The public have not been aware that they have been eating it, it is so similar to the old bread, that the change is' hardly noticeable. "I asked a gentleman friend of mine the other day," writes'our reporter, "whether he had had any of- the ,new.bread yet, and he re- plied that he had not. I then asked him where his people bought -their bread, and he told me that they got it from the firm to which I have' referred. Imagine his surprise when I informed him that he had been eating the bread all the week. • That in itself.: will give us an idea of how small ,the change will be. The new bread is far more 'wholesome than the old, and .will be a -step nearer better health which makes a strong nation."

Obligation On Farmers To Keep Lists.

At Daxesbury Sessions, on Tuesday, George Robinson, Hatton-lane, Hatton, was charged by Acting-Sergeant Worth with having contravened the Defence of the Realm Regula- tions by not having posted in some conspicuous place on his premises the name of any male person between the ages of 18 and 41. The Sergeant deposed that he went to Mr. Robinson's place on the fah November and did not find any notice displayed. He asked defendant if he had any man working for him who was between the.ages of 18 and 41, and he replied that he had not. Witness said, "You have a son," and he replied, "He is just 18." As a matter of fact, the son was 18 last Dec- ember and would be 19 this month.

Defendant said that he had no men working for him and did not think the regulation would refer to his son. , Mr. H. Greenllll (clerk) said these orders were perfectly well-known all over the district. Heaps of farmers had been prosecuted for not having put up these net**. ~Defendant was fined 10s.

div.head: DRINK PERIL.
div.p: THE DRINK PERIL.

The Rev. T. T. James, preaching at Wycliffe Congregational Church last Sunday morning on " The crisis," said that the tremendous changes. that were taking place in the positions of supreme authority and responsibility in:the control of our country might ,carry a very different kind,, of feeling to different indivi- duals. In some quarters they might be wel- comed as' the promise of more effective govern- ment, of greater success, and better days to come; in other quarters they might be viewed both with alarm and uncertainty, as the ex- change of that in which reliance had been put. for that which had all the unpleasantness of doubt about it. He thought it was right to point out how much danger lies behind the present and immediate .moment, danger of disunion and disagreement and the bitterness of personal interests. "Such an experience as that of this past week," said the reverend gentleman, "carries with it the' possibility of our country being rent by discord at the moment when it Mould be Controlled by one concentrated will and purpose. It will need all the gifts of mag- nanimityl and unselfishness and . disinterested loyalty to the land we love if this is to be avoided. It - will need the possession of the spirit- which can sink all personal feeling in the one desire to preserve and safeguard the well-being and the safety of our cherished. home. Wise men will be praying that God will keep us one. And something maybe done to achieve it, not merely by those in high places, but by the simplest and humblest members of the community in the exercise of their. responsibilities. It is one of our deepest needs, and we still therefore ask God for it with all our hearts, this gift of the spirit of unity by which we shall still show one front to the world."

He was no pessimist as to the future, but things had not gone as we wished; the task laid upon us had been heavier than we anti- cipated, and die greatest demands have yet to be made upon us. "1 do not think any of us have 'yet realised this war in this country as we are -going to realise 'it," he continued. " The most exhaustive calls upon our material

resources and upon our :spiritual resources have yet to be made. And sometimes we may be forgiven if we ask ourselves what the spiritual resources ,of our nation really are. For the call to courage and endurance, patience and sacrifice is going to be more complete and vital than it has ever been. It is not merely : questionable whether these things can be found in a people apart from God; it is quite certain that they cannot be. You cannot blot out history. The men who swept the seas. of the Spanish terror, and made the Armada the laughing stock of the world; the men who challenged the divine right of kings, and won the spiritual and religious liberties of England; the men . who rang the' death-knell of a military dictator .as liei :bestrode Europe .a hundred years ago, and banished the threat of national extinction, were men who; sinned they ever so greatly in many things, yet believed in God - and sought His face. div.head: Vicar Satirical About Low Church Ideals.
div.p: Vicar Satirical About Low Church Ideals.

At the annual meeting of the Warrington Branch of the English Church Union, held on Monday. evening, in the, Patten Hall, under the chairmanship of the Rev. Wilfrid J. Stanton, the following officers were elected for the ensuing year :—Chairman, Mr. C. S. Burgess; hon. secretary, Rev. J. H. G. 'nolo lingworth ; hon. treasurer, Mr. E. H. Coates; committee. Rev. C. M. Johnston; Miss White, Mr. W. H. Stansfield and Mr. Thomas, Jackson. The Rev. S. A. Barrett, vicar of St. Ann's, Liverpool, discoursing Upon "The Good Old Low Church Days,' said while there was good and -bad on both sides, where they had the Low Church strong they had the Church ,weak, ,and where they had the High Chard' 'Strong they had the Church strong. too. He in- stanced the case of Sheffield, whiCh was at the bottom in the number of confirmation candi- dates. He was concerned to know how Low Churchism gained any footing in the Church of England; and opined that it was the con- sequence of the Marian persecutions, when a number of our Reformers sought ,refuge On the Continent, where they picked up `` all sorts of Protestant ideals?' They found - the traditional state of things in the reign of Queen Elizabeth. Coming to the great revival of John Wesley, he said it operated outside the Church of England, and, Unfortunately, not inside it. At the beginning of the 19th century, before the Catholic' Revival started, there were about 10,000 parishes in the land, and in 5,000 parishes the clergy were non resident. and there was a district in Liverpool called "The Holy Land," where the clergy lived away from the slumland where their parishioners were. He referred in scathing terms to the conditien of the churches, their neglected 'state, and unentertaining quality of the music, and averred that the Bishops'spent their time in amassing large fortunes for ,themselves and looking* after the welfare of their friends.
The Bev. s. IT. G. Hollingworth moved, and Mr. E. TT. Coates seconded, a vote of thanks to Mr. Barrett for his address.

The qhairman, ,in his farewell address to the union in that capacity, an Office lie had held for ten years, said be had left the die- trict, but hoped to SOP the members from time to time. One of the great works in which the English Church Union could help was to influence the 'people of the country to feel a 'sense of sin—the knowledge of what- God is and what man ought to be. ,What was wanted was real unity—a unity in the faith and agreement in the truth of God's Holy Word. 'A warm' vote' of thanks wii.s-pased to the Eev. W. J. Stanton for his past Services.

On Saturday afternoon Mrs. Parr (Grappen- -11411 HeyS),, a lady whose philanthropic efforts are widely known and highly appreciated in Latchford and, indeed, the whole Warrington district, opened an attractive sale of work in the Parish Room of Christ Church, Latchford. There was a large attendance, including many prominent people of the parish. The Rev. G. C. Briggs; vicar, said that Mrs. Parr needed no introduction to a Latchford gathering, especially those • who attended that 'sale of work, as she came there year after year to support them. It was ten years since she last performed the opening cerenfony at the sale, and although she needed no' introduction, they always gave her a very hearty welcome. The objects of the sale were for the different paro- chial organisations, and they were hoping this year that a grant might be made to .the en- downient of the living. An ' anonymous' donor had made a gift of ..t5O to the endowment fund. Provided this amount was made up to .400; the Ecclesiastical Commissioners would meet it with another £lOO, and if that .1:200 was invested, producing £8 per year,' it would make the living £14.8 instead of £l4O as at present. They did not -keep 'all the money they 'made to them- selves ; they gave some to charitable organisa- tions and institutions. He would mention one well known to all of them—the Warrington Dis- trict Nursing Association. (Applause.) They made a grant to it every year from the sale. The work -of the Association was very much appreciated not only in Latchford, but also in Warrington. It was one of the finest charitable institutions in -the neighbourhood. jlo thanked all those who contributed to the success of the sale, and specially mentioned' the Members of the Church Workers' Association who came there month by month and worked on behalf of the parish. They also thanked the stallholderS and other helper's. (Applause.) Mrs. Parr, in declaring the sale open, said that' it had now been- held for so many years that they might almost call it an. institution. The workers were always ready to keep it going, and their devotion to the parish needs was beyond all praise. (Applause.) She warmly commended the objects of the sale. The Rev. H.. V. Pigot, rector of Grappenhall, proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Parr, and mentioned that that was the 26th occasion on -which he himself was present at the' annual sale, and that was 'the first occasion on which his wife had been absent during the same period. Mr. ,11. Short seconded the vote, which was cordially passed.

The Girl Graduates' Opportunities. The girl graduate of to-day may pick and choose her profession, for her outlook is very different now from What it was in pre-war times. Although the Minister of Munitions is calling aloud for recruits, the girl graduate can do better .vork, and (mite as patriotic in the pro- fessions for which which her higher education fits her. For mathematicians there is a great demand; boys' and girls' schools alike are cry- ing out for teachers; statisticians are in great request for Government and other offices. Engi- neering firms are °florin,'" training for nothing, and a woman has •juas- been appointed over workers of her own sex in a now instructional workshoii fer making the parts of aero-engines; whilst a Manchester firm is paying a woman engineer five pdunds per week. Accountants, banks and commercial houses are all-wanting women, an.l for those with a liking for figures. there is a promising future in the world of finance. The British 'Association employs women investigators of economics, cinemas require cen- sors- under local government bodies,. whilst the number of secretaries for charities, committees, and child-welfare centres is not enough to go round. Winter Colours and Fashions.

A new feature of evening wraps is introduced in the form of curious hems, which to unaccus- tomed eyes are not an. improvement on the old style, which lies flat, whereas the new mode appears to puff out inside and outside, as if they were inflated with air. For evening dresses the sash train has come back again. It consists of a wide handsome ribbon, held at the back in a big how, the ends long enough to..trail, a foot or two on .the ground. Bright colours are, per- missible in the case of children and 'older girls for party wetir,- hut fon, other occasion's; and in the case of 'grown-ups, there is a general feel- ing for trestraint in colours. Serviceable dark and ,lignt greys, ranging from penri to smoke and iron; mastic, beige, and antelope tints will be-worn throughout the winter and the coming spring, for they include in their varions.shades the soft invisible tones of the field uniforms of the Allies, and these will be popular :6's long as the war lasts. New tones. of mole have ap- peared,.. and next to those just .mentioned will come in point of popularity a range of usettil browns, although some are lighter than. 'nigger, the range including bulrush and the rich tones of dark old-fashioned wallflowers. Blues, ex- cept navy, are for a time -Suffering an eclipse; pinks from palest flesh to the deep tones of the cyclamen are favoured, for all tffese contrast well with neutral tones.

To Utilise a Paisley Shawl. An economical wrap is reversible, and can therefore be worn On ono side by day, the other for evening. A lovely model was in black and green, the former satin, with detachable : fur collar, the latter a silk and metal tissue in chrysanthemums and roses. This tissue is used also as a lining for the more expenSive fur coats, since its lightness adds nothing to the weight of the garment. Many evening cloaks of the reversible order are in the old-world Paisley Patterns, indeed these designs .are much. in evi- dence- now in brocades and other materials used for linings, and an old-fashioned Paisley shawl of an attractive pattern, and in a good state of preservation, can be used to advantage by its fortunate possessor. It will ma,ke one side of a reversible evening wrap, that can also be worn during the day time. A new long coat for &din-

ary wear is of soft black satin with a dull rich surface, but the hard brilliant variety of this• fabric does not go well with the fur that trims the garment, nor is it becoming to the wearer. The skirts of the coat are nearly .as long as the dress worn with it, and quite full. The top of the coat often has a Russian blouse effect, and the bands of fur on the skirt may be placed at intervals, instead of going all round, an arrange- ment which makes for economy,'

Roses for Children's Party Frocks. Children's frocks for Christmas parties are, even in war time, claiming attention, fer the festival that belongs especially to.the little ones must be kept with as many old-time ceremonies as the war will permit. There is a number of charming- materials to choose from, and almost as many styles—all equally attractive. Georgette crepe, a very, thin, almost transparent crepe de chine, that nevertheless wears and washes well, chiffon, spotted net, muslin white and coloured, and that old friend, thin Japanese silk, are but a few ,of the fabrics offered this season. A new departure that is used on dresses of distinctly different types, is the ribbon belt, which appears to be preferred just now to the sash to give relief to a white frock, but this does not mean that the sash has disappeared: it is still very much in evidence. Flowers, always so suitable for children; -aro .vetT pret- tily used on plain muslin frocks, they form the belts, and decorate the necks and sleeves, and are used to simulate pockets on the skirts. , The rosebuds are quite flat, and arranged in ropes. Little frocks, like big ones, may be fussy or plain, according to .the tastes of the mother. Some charming silk models have flounces zof lace on the skirts between cordings.of silk, and quaint fichn bodices that finish at the belted waist. Potatoes In Their Skins.

A great national economy may he secured, ready to hand, by the use of a little. Common sense, viz.: Let the extravagant practice ef. peeling potatoes be abolished. It would sur- prise the public if they realised how much of the nutriment is extracted by the present pray.- tics of opening the starch-cells with a knife (i.e., what peeling amounts to), and then sub- jebting them to the effects of boiling water for, say; twenty minutes. . No benefit is •gained that cannot be secured by even simpler means, for when unpeeled potatoes have been boiled for, say, five min- utes, the water may be poured off, and tne skins can then be* taken off without loss; thus a potato still hard and firm is secured, freed of its, skin, and ,suitable, for preparing potato chips 'and scoresi of other ifems.. Or Allis par- tially boiled potato,' after being freect-•of its skin, may be replaced into the boiling water and further cooked into potato meal or flour for mash, soups, cakes, &c. If peeling potatoes be abolished, it need not lessen their use for any purpose, but it would ensure a Vast "econ- omy. equal, at least, to increasing the potato yield by one-tenth. Dietists teach us that, as in wheat, 60 in potatoes, the most nourishing portions are those in contact with the 'skin. Stewed Tripe. _ _

Serve very hot and garnished with neat pieces of toast.

div.head: SCIENCE AND INDUSTRY.
div.p: SCIENCE AND INDUSTRY.
Britain Behind The Times, But , Progressing.
HINTS REGARDING THE SECONDARY. SCHOOL

Dr. T. P. Ililditeh, research chemist at :Messrs. Joseph Crosiield and Sons; Ltd., greatly. interested members of the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society, on Mon- day eveuing, by a lecture on "Science and Industry," with special reference to that of the chemical and allied industries. Ile made some valuable liggestions, particularly re- m-arding the classes held at the. Secondary hool.

By the public at large, he began, chemistry had been neglected, and it was only recently that, when they found supplies of their favourite art shades and many of their nar- cotic and other, for cut off: and there was a great demand or shells and accompanying modern high explosives, they realised of what importance the industry was. In applied chemistry Britain had fallen behind, because of (1): lack of enterprise and foresight (:n the next ef the chemical manufacturer; (2) in- sufficient pay; and (3) lack of educational facilities for chemists. Ho was, however, of opinion that although Germany had more chemists than we, ours were on the average of higher ability. (Applause.) Was it too late to improve chemical educa- tion now? It wa.s very difficult to say, but any attempt must be by drastic and costly reforms. It was eclipse or Empire, and, therefore, a plain duty to make the attempt. We had a very fine secondary day school in Warrington, but obviously it could never edu- cate all those who took up chemical work in the varions factories. The education of the typical works chemist in technical -.chemistry would commence generally just after he had left school and began to work, and would be by evening work. There was an admirably arranged course in general chemistry at War- rington for evening education of secondary school students Who went, into works. It was spread over a number of years; too many, in• fact, lie thought that if .the general course could be shortened by a year or two, and final specialised courses substituted for students engaged in particular works, the students would gain enormously in individual value; as would also .the works, and, there- fore, the town. Warrington was a kern of many industries; in point of fact they were nearly all chemical. There was room for half a dozen specialised courses of literally vital importance to thousands of our citizens; there was urgent need for at least three or four; yet there was not one. It meant addiional expense, of course; but it was not a very expensive side of technical education. It was not, instruction in the secrets of the rawest trade processes by ex- perts who would want a big fee to talk, but each branch of applied chemist*- had its own modified methods of analytical and other prac- tical work, which mild rapidly be picked up by a special course if the general one :were concluded when the application of general principles to the routine work of a particular branch completed the educathin of the modern works' chemist.

div.head: LESSON FROM LONDON.
div.p: A LESSON FROM LONDON.

In an evening college—very similar to that at Warrington—with which he was associated some time ago, a number of those courses were held and several of them were in charge of former students engaged during the day in. the work of their subjects—students who, in passing through -their general course, attracted the attention of the head (A their department by their abilities, and were sub- sequently asked to lecture on the routine of their own branch. The plan worked very Well and was cheap. That particular school in. the London neighbonrhood was only one of per- haps six or eight similar institutions within a radius of four miles of it. There were many small factories of various. industries in the neighbourhood, but rarely • approaching the sim or .importance of several of our works Mire. Yet the classes were well attended, and the annual entry of students (new and Old) in the chemical department was, when he last heard it, three or four hundred, and was show- ing a consistent annual increase. rheC.OlClllO of the general evening ebemistry course here—if he might be permitted to coin- ment upon it—was quite admirable, loaf its utility was lal-gely restricted to those who had passed through the Secondary School, or who had been amongst the brightest of the eletneuT tary scholars. At present it failed absolutely to do anything for those who found themselves in works, with no knowledge of chemistry, and who felt they would increase their own value (and- who, in fact, would 1* of more use to their musters) if they had some intelligent idea of what they were doing.. There were far more who would be willing to learn the elements of their work In that way than one might ever have imagined; but those men, some of them far beyond school age, would not consent to devote several evenings per week to subjects which they could see were not of direct use to them, and met with a refusal unless they agreed to the complete eciurse, and, in addi- tion, a qualifying course of one year's dura- tion. Discouraged, they: chucked up Any idea of evening education, while in Other instances saddled themselves with the price of a contract ticket to the nearest town where facilities for such cases were provided. The complete course ',Totem was, he knew, far the better if it were taken at the right age, but he had already pointed out that the Secondary School could not provide sufficient works' chemists for the town in any case; and, if it could, was War- rington to wait half a generation until the system was in full working order?

div.p: FIFTY YEARS BEHIND.

British chemical industry WWI already fifty years behind the times. Warrington, of course. was not the only industrial town which suffered from over-emphasis of a complete:•course of study, which only.a fraction of those who should be evening students could pursue, and the responsibility did not largely rest, one felt sure, with the local authorities who supervised education, but with those at Whitehall. , Mr. C. E. Parker seconded, and first ex- pressed the hope that the 'Doctor was too pessimistic when lie said that we were fifty years behind in the matter of chemistry. However terrible the disadvantages of the War In its many aspects, it was rather pleasing to think that there were some little compensat- ing things that were accruing to us. • One of those was that we had been awakened to our deficiencies. It was. surprising what advances had been made in industry, chemical and otherwise, during the last two or three years. The progress had been really marvellous. We had become alive to the fact that in some respects Germany was very much ahead. Many of the enemy's claims had proved to be false, but not all. Looking back over his own time he could remember the first introduction of chemistry to the tanning trade, and with what suspicion the chemist was viewed—and he deserved to be, too. - (Laughter.) Those conditions had now passed away, and, as far as the ,chemistry of tanning was con- cerned, at any rate, England stood ahead of the whole world. (Applause.) The walking s ticks, provided for wounded soldiers and sailors by Mr. 'Stewart Royston, Sunnyside, Paddington, Warrington, are helping to comfort men from all parts of the world, and Mr. Royston's fund quite naturally is being sup- ported from all quarters. I am writing to them to say I am giv- ing them ten walking sticks, and telling you to give them away where needed. But it is their gift. as I am not giving Christmas toys and fancies this year." Would- they .be kind enough to give these little affairs round to any of the Australians they come across? We had some pressed wattle, and I made these up a day or two ago, thinking they may give a tiny bit of pleasure to an Australian in greeting him with a piece of the national flowfr here, wattle, at Christmas time." Sir Charles Russell, chairman Collection Com- mittee of the British' Red Cross Society, writing to Mr. Stewart Royston under recent date, says: "May I beg to echo the .wish that Ton may be able to continue the kind and excellent work you are doing on behalf of the wounded soldiers. The two thousand Wounded soldiers who have received walking,stieks in the Lord Derby War Hospital, and the Whlteeross Military Hospital, Redden Court Red Cross Hospital and the Thel- wall Heys C.Amvalescent Home—it is here where heartfelt gratitude knows no bounds. Miss Margaret Broadbent, commandan t of Padden Court, Red Cross Hospital, Latchford, writes :—" Please accept the warm thanks of the patients and of myself for the-fiplendid gift of 100 walking sticks, which have arrived "safely, and for which we are most grateful." Mr. Arthur Bottotuley, on behalf of the com- mittee of the Whitecross Military Hospital, writes to Mr. Royston thanking him very heartily for the kind gift of 100 walking sticks gentler the patiente, and assures him that his kindness will be much appreciated by the men." As 'Warrington military hospitals have been benefiting SO largely through the Walking Stick Fund, we trust our readers who have not already done so; will give their support. • One thousand walking sticks wero asked for recently, and of that number six hundred have passed into these " havens of peace," where they are so welcome.

div.head: FORTY-FIVE SHILLING GUARANTEE
div.p: THE FORTY-FIVE SHILLING GUARANTEE

This is finding favour in ,unexpected quar- ters. The " Daily Chronicle" says: "In face of the new situation confronting us, ought not the .question of a"State guarantee of prices for a definite term to be reconsidered by the Gov- ernment? It seems absurd to suggest that a guarantee of 455. a quarter would be an in- .ducement to farmers to put more land under the plough when wheat prices are soaring above 70s. a quarter. But it has to be borne in mind that what the farmer requires is seeurity. There is no asiiurance that high prices will continue; they may fall during the war; they will certainly drop when the war is over, though it is improbable that they will ever sink again to the low 'levels of the '9o's. A farmer already at his wits' end for labour cannot be expected to change his whole system of cultivation without any protection against the risk of wheat Prices tumbling down. That is why a minimum price should be guaranteed for a term pf years. Such a guarantee would give the farmer security and confidence. Other corn crops, such as oats and barley, stand, of course, in the same position as wheat. Lord Miler's Committee expressed the opinion that the policy of a State minimum price would lead to an increased production of wheat in this country., Even if this prediction were not realised the experiment would be worth trying.
