div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.
NEWLY-PLANTED FRUIT TREES AND
MANURE.

Many people run away . with the idea that the addition of manure to the soil when fruit trees are being planted is necessary. NO greater mistake can be made, as the Use of manure only causes a gross growth .which will never do any good so far as cropping is con- cerned. Should the soil into which the fruit trees are to be put be poor, then far better is it to remove such soil and fill in the space with some good fibrous loam, which will ans- wer for several years. Then when the trees have got \ a good hold, and are growing freely, a mulch of rotten- manure may be laid on the surface to encourage the formation of fibrins roots, the mainstay of the tree. Another fault of adding manure- to the soil is that the roots go down deeply, failure soon or later following, and necessitating root pruning. For the amateur with a small garden, trees-, on the paradise are .the best, as on this stock they very soon come into ebearing, while, when the fruit is swelling, it ía an easy matter to give them a mulch of manure or apply liquid manure in some form.'

div.head: OUTDOOR CHRYSANTHEMUMS.
div.p: OUTDOOR CHRYSANTHEMUMS.

In many districts these will not survive the winter; hence it is advisable 'to lift the stools now that flowering is over, and lay them in a frame or a temporary boarded-in erection, so that a supply of young' plants may be forth- coming for next year's display. Those who may not have any convenience as above noted may, with sonie hope of success, loosen the plants with a fork, and raise them slightly. This will prevent the water lying round the stools, which, if heavy rains prevail, render the surrounding soil water-logged, and kill the plants. We' have found it a good plan when the stools have been raised in the way alluded to above to sprinkle some coal ashes that have been exposed to the air for some time, this covering protecting from frost, and at the same. time-warding off slugs, which eat off the young shoots as they come through the soil. In many villa and country gardens a small glass-house exists. Than .this there is no better place for keeping the old stools, which may be laid into some lrght sandy soil, and stood on the stage or placed in boxes. Given this attention the plants keep well through the winter, and by the spring are bristling with young shoots with • roots attached, which may be potted up or put into boxes and grown on to put out in May. grow a number of these, and find no difficulty in keeping the old; stools, which I stand on a bed of ashes in a frame and cover with cocoa fibre. In the country, there is always plenty of leaf soil, which answers the same purpose.— "Wick," in "Farm and Home."

Bad the presence of these two players alone been known it would have been the means of a larger attendance of spectators. The game proved to be one of the best witnessed since the Town Club was formed, and the specta- tors were well satisfied with the result.

The visitors commenced operations by show- ing good combination, low ground passes being a feature of their game. The home team were not slow to show their abilities in the same direction and proved more consistent in their attacks, but so strong was the defence of the visitors - that it was nearly half-time before' the first point was registered. Play had been in progress about twenty minutes when it was seen that the home captain had changed the positions of some of his team, Siddall ;going to the outside position on the right, ,Owen coming to the half-back line, and ,Banner going forward. These changes were wisely made and strengthened both the ,ittack and defence of Warrington, and re- sulted in Illidge scoring the first goal for the Town. Before this Siddall had, to the spec- tators' ,point of view, two or three easy open- ings, but always found Hanna in the way of his progress, and the latter on several occa- sions had made some very smart saves. The second portion opened very keenly and was very much appreciated by the spectators. This exciting period was followed by a good j spell of even play, in which both defences were prominent, and as the final stages were entered upon aiddall scored for the home team, and a couple of minutes before time Hanna scored j for the visitors from a penalty kick.

The spectators were well satisfied with the display of both teams, but the score ought to have been more in favour of the home team, as there were f,everal openings which ought to have been easily scored from.

We all deal with destiny, wittingly or not. He who had been Arthur Stanleigh and John Powell, alike wastrel and profligate, and yet fondly be- loved, had mounted the stairway of the wind and rode upon the wings of the morning, without fear and without hope. He had dealt with destiny and had won. By some miracle of the commonplace, the falling aeroplane had struck a low, thick, sturdy tree, and the man plunging to death had been thrown up into 'the canvas wing of the bird- machine, and so, saved by the jar, had escaped unharmed. The wondering gipsies chafad:• his hands and brow; one put a brandy flash between his lips and forced a few of its fiery drops between the clenched teeth. They bore Arthur back to the gipay camp near by in wondering silence, and then Esther relieved the gipsy woman watching by the couch of Hagar and whispered to the dying woman, "Can you bear a great happiness?" A smile transfigured the wan face of Hagar. "I know the good news you bring," she murmured. "Arthur. my dear son, is here." Prescient in the face of death, Hagar also knew that the husk of evil had fallen from Arthur, and that the wings of the morning had wafted clean strength to his soul. He leaned his head against that loving, tired breast and knew—full, deep„ and satisfying—that a mother's prayer was indeed a charm against harm, .above all diamonds. In those few moments of 'deep rapture Hagar,, realised at last that her sorrows and sacrifices had not been in, vain. Her son, parted from her since his birth hour, was in her arms at last, the man she had always hoped he would grow to be. This was the news that Quabba came sadly back to find. This was the news that wrenched his faithful humble soul. But Esther and Arthur -did not weep. They felt that Hagar had passed in joy beyond comprehension, and Esther had no cause for tears and Arthur had cause too deep for them. They gazed • upon the calm face of Hagar hand in, hand, while Arthur pledged his vows again to be whole of heart and body as the dead would wish. After Hagar had been laid to rest the gipsies led by Arthur, now calling himself by the name of Harding, journeyed back to fair Virginia to their mountain rendezvous in the _Blue Ridge., The -journey was long and slow and yet a happy one for the fond lovers. As if in truth the evil husk had fallen from him in the plunge from the clouds that Blair's treacherous tampering with the aero- plane had caused, Arthur had found the drug habit and its desire pass from him. If it was by a struggle with the flesh, he did not show it. His eyes grew bright; his tanned face glowed with happiness, and ever through the sun and shade Esther, his beloved, rode by his side, her tender hand in his. Esther had made her choice. "Shall we, dear, go back to Stanleigh Hall or stay with our people?" "I never knew a happy day there, Arthur. Let us stay with our giPsY People." "We will, darling. Wealth and luxury do not bring happiness." One day, before the wedding which united two loving hearts, Tom Blake rode over to the Blue Ridge bringing proof of Blair Stanleigh's guilt. Blake pleaded with Arthur to halt Blair in the hour of his supposed triumph, but /Esther and Arthur refused. "Let Blair have the Powell rail- lions; let him have Stanleigh Hall; let him have the Earldom in England and The Diamond from the Sky," said Arthur. "We have more than all these things, for in casting them aside we have found love and happiness."

"Your mother, Hagar Harding, was my best friend. She gave Me my start in life,"#said Blake, huskily. "I will abide by your wish. Abe Bloom suspects much but knows little regarding Blair Stanleigh. Bloom dare not move unless I say so, and I can hold him quiet. Even near Fairfax you will never be recognised in the gipsy, Arthur Hard- ing, by the people who knew you as Arthur Stan- leigh. The few short years have changed you, but it is different with Miss Esther Stanleigh here. Who could not tell hey? You cannot keep the secret on this account. I know." "This is a sheltered place which only the gipsies know the way to; knly the gipsies, with the excep- tion of yourself," replied Arthur. "You know the way because my mother taught you, and you know the Romany password which admits you past the outer vans. This is the old rendezvous of my mother. The gipsies own the very land. We will not be here long—only for our wedding, which will be a gipsy one. ',None but a Romany can be at the wedding; none but you, for you were adopted into the tribe as a boy. I am told." _ .

Wesley Guild.—A very interesting lecture on "Dr. Johnson" was given in the Guild Bodin on Thursday evening by the Bev. W. T. Derry, of Warrington. He gave a graphic de- scription of Dr. Johnson's life, showing how, in spite of adversity, his disposition was one of generosity and kindness. He was also full off• wit and humour, his repartee being very racy. .1-le made' many friends and kept them. His last days were full of suffering, and the walls of .
